data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The single best cross-city modulator of the nocturnal UHI is city size itself: larger cities have a greater aggregate thermal mass and a deeper, more persistent urban heat island because the volume of stored heat scales with impervious surface area, and the resulting warm dome is thicker and more resistant to nocturnal cooling.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If a small, extremely dense city (e.g., Hong Kong) has a larger nocturnal UHI than a large, low-density city (e.g., Los Angeles), city size is not the primary modulator.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If coastal breezes or regional winds ventilate large cities more effectively than small cities in sheltered valleys, the scaling with size would break down.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If built density and sky view explain the variance better than total area, city size is a proxy rather than the mechanism.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The total heat stored during daytime is proportional to the impervious surface area and thermal mass of urban materials. Larger cities accumulate more total heat, and the urban boundary layer dome that forms over them is deeper. After sunset, this larger heat reservoir releases sensible heat over a longer period, sustaining nocturnal warming. The cross-city gap scales with city size because the total heat storage and boundary layer depth increase with the horizontal extent of the urban area.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
